Следующая техника помогает работать с самокритикой, предлагая вам стать собственным адвокатом. Может показаться необычным, но она удивительно эффективна.

Чтобы ослабить влияние критических мыслей, важно не только замечать их, но и уметь уверенно им противостоять.

Представьте, что вы будто оказались в суде. В роли обвинителя — ваши внутренние критические мысли, которые уже давно ставят вам ярлыки: «неудачник», «слабый», «виноват во всём».

Но теперь у вас появляется роль защитника. Ваша задача — оспорить обвинения, показать, что они необоснованны и искажены.

<q author="Элизабет Гилберт">Будьте адвокатом своего внутреннего мира, а не судьёй собственной истории.</q>

Представьте себя компетентным адвокатом. Вы не ограничитесь фразой «я хороший» — вы будете приводить реальные факты, логичные аргументы и здравые объяснения.

Это работа с внутренним диалогом на уровне доказательств, а не эмоций.

Ниже пример того, как это может выглядеть на практике:
en.oldText:
The following technique helps you work with self-criticism by inviting you to become your own advocate. It may sound unusual, but it’s surprisingly effective.

To weaken the impact of critical thoughts, it’s important not only to notice them but also to counter them with confidence.

Imagine you’re in a courtroom. Your inner critical thoughts play the role of the prosecutor, assigning labels like “failure,” “weak,” or “to blame for everything.”

Now you take on the role of the defense. Your task is to dispute the charges and show that they’re unfounded and distorted.

Picture yourself as a competent attorney. You won’t stop at “I’m a good person”—you’ll bring real facts, logical arguments, and sound explanations.

This is an inner dialogue grounded in evidence, not emotion.

en.newText:
The following technique helps you work through self-criticism by encouraging you to become your own advocate. It might sound unusual, but it’s surprisingly effective.

To weaken the influence of critical thoughts, it’s important not only to notice them but also to know how to stand up to them with confidence.

The prosecutor is your inner critic, which has long been labeling you as a “failure,” “weak,” or “guilty.”

But now, you have the role of the defense attorney. Your task is to challenge the accusations and show that they are unfounded and distorted.

<q author="Elizabeth Gilbert">Be an advocate for your inner world, not a judge of your own story.</q>

Picture yourself as a competent lawyer. You won’t just say “I’m good”—you will present real facts, logical arguments, and sound explanations.

This is about managing your inner dialogue using evidence rather than emotions.

Imagine you often criticize yourself, calling yourself weak and a failure. Now try stepping into the role of the defense—even if it feels difficult at first.

The goal is to defend yourself honestly, thoughtfully, and respectfully, as if you were defending someone you care about.

A psychologist suggests an exercise:

All right, let’s try a role-play. I’ll be the prosecutor and you’ll be the defense attorney.

Ready? Let’s begin.

(Prosecutor) Paul is weak and a failure; nothing he does works out.

(Defense) That’s not accurate. Paul earned a degree, has achieved career milestones, and is surrounded by people who value him.

(Prosecutor) But he makes mistakes and doesn’t always handle things well—so he’s still a failure.

(Defense) Mistakes are part of every human life. They don’t define a person or prove incompetence.

(Prosecutor) Fine. But he’s weak.

(Defense) Do you have evidence? Paul works hard, makes decisions, and handles difficulties. His efforts show the opposite.

(Prosecutor) He could try harder.

(Defense) If he truly lacked diligence, he wouldn’t be valued at work or considered for promotion. The claim is unfounded.

Попробуйте несколько простых упражнений:

«Срывание ярлыков»

Представьте, что люди вокруг ходят с ярлыками на лбу («неудачник», «ленивый», «некрасивая» и т. д.). Каждый раз, когда замечаете такой ярлык у себя в голове, мысленно снимайте его.

«Коробка ярлыков»

Возьмите коробку и стикеры. Каждый раз, когда ловите себя на ярлыке, запишите его и положите в коробку. В конце недели — выбросьте содержимое. Можно делать это и в заметках телефона. «Замена ярлыков»

Попробуйте заменить негативный ярлык на нейтральное или позитивное качество.

Например, вместо «тупой» — «учусь», вместо «ленивый» — «утомлён, нуждаюсь в отдыхе». Это может показаться непривычным, но помогает развивать доброжелательность и реальное видение. Главная идея — не заменять ярлык на другой, а постепенно отказываться от категоричных оценок и видеть человека, а не одно слово. Чем меньше мы живём через ярлыки, тем легче замечаем настоящую многогранность себя и других.
en.oldText:
Try a few simple exercises:

“Peeling Off Labels”

Imagine people walking around with labels on their foreheads (“loser,” “lazy,” “unattractive,” etc.). Each time you notice such a label in your mind, take it off mentally.

“Label Box”

Take a box and some sticky notes. Each time you catch yourself labeling, write it down and drop it in the box. At the end of the week, throw them all away.

You can do this in your phone notes, too.

“Replacing Labels”

Try swapping a negative label for a neutral or positive quality.

For example, instead of “stupid,” say “learning”; instead of “lazy,” try “tired and in need of rest.”

It may feel unfamiliar at first, but it builds kindness and a more accurate view.

The main goal isn’t to trade one label for another, but to gradually let go of categorical judgments and see the person—not a single word.

The fewer labels we live by, the easier it becomes to notice the true complexity in ourselves and others.

Try these simple exercises:

“Unlabeling”

Imagine that people around you are walking around with labels on their foreheads (“failure,” “lazy,” “unattractive,” etc.). Every time you notice such a label popping up in your head, mentally strip it away.

“The Label Box”

Take a box and some sticky notes. Every time you catch yourself using a label, write it down and put it in the box. At the end of the week, throw the contents away. You can also do this in your phone’s notes app. “Replacing Labels”

Try replacing a negative label with a neutral or positive quality.

For example, instead of “stupid,” try “learning”; instead of “lazy,” try “exhausted, needs rest.” This might feel unfamiliar at first, but it helps develop kindness and a more realistic perspective. The main goal isn’t just to swap one label for another, but to gradually move away from categorical judgments and see the person, not just a single word. The less we live through labels, the easier it becomes to notice the true complexity of ourselves and others.

en.ru:
Почему мотивация так и не появляется?

Часто нам кажется, что без желания мы ничего не сможем сделать.

Но действительно ли в жизни всё происходит только из-за мотивации? Всегда ли вы идёте на работу с энтузиазмом? Или иногда — потому что нужно?

Когда мы говорим «у меня нет мотивации», это часто значит: «я не хочу» или «мне тяжело начать».

Это нормально. Мы не обязаны хотеть всё, что полезно.

При депрессии почти ничего не хочется. Хочется лежать, исчезнуть, спрятаться. Но долгие периоды бездействия только усиливают страдания.

Парадокс в том, что мотивация часто появляется уже после действия, а не до него.
en.oldText:
Why doesn’t motivation show up?

We often assume that without desire, we can’t do anything.

But does everything in life really happen only because of motivation? Do you always go to work with enthusiasm—or sometimes simply because it’s needed?

When we say “I have no motivation,” it often means “I don’t want to” or “it’s hard to start.”

That’s normal. We don’t have to want everything that’s good for us.

In depression, almost nothing feels appealing. You want to lie down, disappear, hide. But long stretches of inaction only deepen the suffering.

The paradox is that motivation often appears after action, not before it.
en.newText:
Why doesn’t motivation appear?

We often feel that we can’t do anything without the desire to do it.

But does everything in life really depend on motivation? Do you always go to work with enthusiasm? Or sometimes, do you go simply because you have to?

When we say “I have no motivation,” we often actually mean “I don’t want to” or “it’s hard for me to start.”

That’s okay. We aren’t required to want everything that is beneficial for us.

During depression, you may feel like doing almost nothing. You might want to lie down, disappear, or hide. However, long periods of inactivity only intensify the suffering.

The paradox is that motivation often appears *after* action, rather than before it.

en.ru:
Навешивание ярлыков — это когда мы даём себе или другому человеку категоричную, негативную оценку на основании одного события или поступка, без глубокого анализа и учёта контекста. Люди больше всего на свете любят наклеить на другого человека ярлык, который раз и навсегда освобождает их от необходимости думать. Например:
  • Опоздал на встречу — безответственный
  • Сделал что-то для себя — эгоист
  • Лежит на диване в выходной — лентяй
  • Не сдал экзамен — тупой
  • Уволили с работы — неудачник
    • Такая реакция напоминает способ мышления детей: когда они только учатся понимать мир и стремятся быстро упорядочить новую информацию. Но взрослый человек уже способен смотреть шире и анализировать ситуацию, а не делать выводы по одному эпизоду.
en.oldText:
Labeling is when we assign a categorical, negative judgment to ourselves or someone else based on a single event or action, without deeper analysis or context.

For example:

Late to a meeting — irresponsible

Put themselves first — selfish

Lying on the couch on a day off — lazy

Failed an exam — stupid

Got fired — loser

This kind of reaction resembles a child’s thinking: they’re still learning how the world works and try to sort new information quickly.

Adults, however, can take a broader view and analyze the situation instead of drawing conclusions from a single moment.
en.newText:
Labeling is when we give ourselves or others a categorical, negative assessment based on a single event or action, without deep analysis or considering the context. People love nothing more than to label another person, freeing themselves once and for all from the need to think. For example:
  • Late for a meeting — irresponsible
  • Doing something for yourself — selfish
  • Lying on the couch on a weekend — lazy
  • Failed an exam — stupid
  • Got fired — a loser
    • This reaction is similar to how children think: they are just learning to understand the world and try to quickly organize new information. But as adults, we are capable of seeing the bigger picture and analyzing a situation rather than jumping to conclusions based on a single episode.

Во время депрессии начать что-то делать бывает особенно сложно. Кажется, что мотивация должна появиться первой, но она не приходит. Вы будто впадаете в «зимнюю спячку» и ждёте, что наступит день, когда всё станет легче само собой.

Мысли вроде «ничего не принесёт удовольствия» или «я всё равно не справлюсь» могут полностью парализовать активность.

<important>В итоге вы всё больше отдаляетесь от привычной жизни, друзей, семьи, любимых занятий. Появляется чувство беспомощности, растёт самокритика — и состояние ухудшается.</important>

Так формируется замкнутый круг.

Но его можно разорвать.

Сначала важно понять природу бездействия при депрессии, а затем познакомиться с техниками, которые помогут вернуть способность действовать.

Один из самых коварных эффектов депрессии — она словно «отключает» волю. Непростые дела откладываются, а прокрастинация становится привычной реакцией.

Каждая задача кажется слишком сложной, мотивации нет — и появляется желание просто ничего не делать.

Чем дольше это продолжается, тем труднее сделать первый шаг. Такое состояние может затягиваться на недели, месяцы и даже годы.

en.oldText:
In depression, getting started can feel especially hard. It seems motivation should come first, but it rarely does. You slip into a kind of “winter hibernation,” waiting for a day when everything gets easier on its own.

Thoughts like “Nothing will bring me pleasure” or “I’ll fail anyway” can freeze you in place.

As a result, you drift further from daily life, friends, family, and the things you used to enjoy. Helplessness grows, self-criticism intensifies—and the depression deepens.

This is how a vicious cycle forms.

But it can be broken.

First, understand the nature of inaction in depression—and then learn techniques that help you regain the ability to act.

One of depression’s most insidious effects is that it seems to “switch off” your will. Difficult tasks get postponed, and procrastination becomes the default.

Every task feels too hard, motivation is absent—and the urge to do nothing takes over.

The longer this lasts, the harder the first step becomes. This state can drag on for weeks, months, even years.

<important>As a result, you drift further away from your usual life, friends, family, and hobbies. A sense of helplessness sets in, self-criticism grows, and your condition worsens.</important>

This creates a vicious cycle.

But it can be broken.

First, it is important to understand the nature of inactivity during depression, and then to learn techniques that can help you regain your ability to act.

One of the most insidious effects of depression is that it feels as if it “switches off” your will. Complex tasks are put off, and procrastination becomes a habitual response.

Every task feels overwhelming, motivation is absent, and you feel a strong urge to simply do nothing.

The longer this continues, the harder it becomes to take that first step. This state can drag on for weeks, months, or even years.

en.oldText:
Here’s an example of a conversation with a psychologist about motivation:

You used to go to the gym regularly, and now you don’t feel drawn to it?

Yes, I just don’t want to.

What if you imagined going to the gym without motivation—simply because you decided to? Then what?

I’d probably start feeling better during the workout.

Exactly. Sometimes action creates motivation—not the other way around. You can feel tired or empty and still take a step—and get a result.

Recall moments when you did something without wanting to but felt better afterward—that experience is familiar.

When we tell ourselves, “I can’t start until I feel like it,” we get stuck. In reality, the desire very often comes after the first step.

Action generates motivation.

We’ve already noted that thoughts influence emotions, and emotions influence behavior. Change your thoughts, and new emotions—and the energy to act—can follow.

You can exit the vicious circle of inaction by gradually stepping into a cycle of activity and recovery.

Каждый человек — это сложная, изменчивая и живая система. Наше поведение зависит от возраста, настроения, обстоятельств, фазы жизни и сотен других факторов.

<important>Попытка описать человека одним ярлыком — как попытка пересказать целый фильм одним кадром: почти всё важное остаётся за кадром.</important>

Навешивание ярлыков на себя — особенно разрушительно. Это лишает нас гибкости, мешает видеть наши сильные стороны и развиваться.

Когда мы навешиваем ярлыки на других, мы рискуем увидеть только одну грань человека и пропустить всё остальное, что делает его живым и уникальным.

Это может привести к конфликтам, недопониманию и отчуждению — ведь никому не приятно быть загнанным в рамки.

<instagram ids="18055242047218399">

Что помогает вместо этого? Замечать факты, которые противоречат ярлыку, и учитывать разные стороны человека.

Например, кто-то резко вошёл в очередь, и первая мысль: «какой хам».

Настроение портится автоматически.

Но если дать себе секунду и предположить, что у человека могла быть срочная причина или тяжёлый день, эмоции становятся мягче, а вывод — менее категоричным.
en.oldText:
Every person is a complex, dynamic, living system. Our behavior depends on age, mood, circumstances, life stage, and hundreds of other factors.

Trying to describe a person with a single label is like retelling an entire film from a single frame: almost everything important stays off-screen.

Labeling yourself is especially destructive. It robs you of flexibility and keeps you from seeing your strengths and growing.

When we label others, we risk seeing only one facet of a person and missing everything else that makes them vivid and unique.

This can lead to conflict, misunderstanding, and distance—no one likes being boxed in.

What helps instead? Notice facts that contradict the label and consider different facets of a person.

For instance, someone cuts in line and your first thought is, “What a jerk.”

Your mood sours instantly.

But if you pause for a second and consider that they might have an urgent reason or be having a rough day, your emotions soften and your conclusion becomes less absolute.

Labeling ourselves is especially destructive. It robs us of flexibility, prevents us from seeing our strengths, and hinders our growth.

When we label others, we risk seeing only one side of them and missing everything else that makes them human and unique.

Your mood automatically drops.

en.oldText:
Inaction is a curious paradox of human nature.

You’ve likely noticed that some people strive to live actively, try new things, and move forward, while others keep their distance from life, as if watching from the sidelines.

Here’s an interesting fact: if a person is isolated and deprived of their usual activity, signs of depression will almost inevitably appear after a while.

In depression, something similar happens—only voluntarily and gradually. It’s as if you sentence yourself to inaction. But do you truly want to live that way?

The thinking pattern in depression often looks like this:

I think about something I could do.

“It’s too hard / I won’t manage / I’ll feel bad / no one needs me.”

Sadness, anxiety, hopelessness.

Inaction or postponing.

Thus a vicious circle forms: negative thoughts → heavy emotions → inaction → even less pleasure and energy → worsening depression.

Inactivity is a striking paradox of human nature.

With depression, the same thing happens, but it feels voluntary and gradual—as if you are sentencing yourself to inactivity. But is this truly how you want to live?

The thought pattern during depression often looks like this:

<step title="common.event">I think about a task I could do.</step>

<step title="common.automatic">“It’s too hard / I won’t succeed / I’ll feel bad / I’m not needed by anyone.”</step>

<step title="common.emotions">Sadness, anxiety, hopelessness.</step>

<step title="common.behavior">Inactivity or procrastination.</step>

This forms a vicious cycle: negative thoughts → heavy emotions → inactivity → even less pleasure and energy → worsening depression.

This technique works because many people find it easier to defend someone else than themselves. Here, you learn to become your own ally.

As the defense, you check facts, demand evidence, and don’t let baseless criticism pass as truth.

When negative thoughts arise, ask: “How would I defend someone I want to support?”

Approach it professionally: analyze, test the logic, and look for facts.

Here are helpful questions:

What is the charge? What exactly are my thoughts “accusing” me of?

Is there real evidence, or is this emotion talking?

What facts speak in my favor?

Can the situation be explained differently—in a kinder, fairer way?

What would a reasonable person do in my place?

Are there external circumstances that influenced what happened?

What can I say in my defense? Which qualities and achievements can I present as arguments?
en.newText:
This technique works because many people find it easier to defend others than themselves. In this case, you are learning to become an ally to yourself. As an advocate, you examine the facts, demand evidence, and refuse to let unfounded criticism sound like the truth. When negative thoughts about yourself arise, try asking: “How would I defend someone I wanted to support?” Approach this like a professional: analyze, check the logic, and look for facts. Here are some questions to help:
  • What is the accusation? What am I being “accused” of by my thoughts?
  • Is there real evidence, or is this just emotion?
  • What facts support my side?
  • Can I explain the situation differently, in a kinder and fairer way?
  • How would a reasonable person in my position act?
  • Are there external circumstances that influenced the situation?
  • What can I say in my defense? What qualities and achievements can I use as arguments?
